1.translation: Thus, first, with “you grieve for those who are not to be grieved,” discrimination between the body and the Self was taught as a means to liberation. Immediately afterward, with “this understanding has been taught to you in Sāṅkhya; hear this one in yoga,” action was also taught. Yet the relation of primary and secondary between the two was not clearly shown. Because the person endowed with understanding—the sthitaprajña—is described as desireless, with controlled senses, without ego, and the teaching is praised in the conclusion “this is the Brahmī state,” Arjuna supposes that the Lord regards understanding as superior between understanding and action. He says: “If understanding is superior to action, being more inwardly connected with liberation, and is approved by you, then why do you repeatedly tell me ‘fight’ and ‘therefore rise,’ and make me engage in this terrible, violent action?”

2.translation: One may object: “In ‘for a kṣatriya there is nothing higher than a righteous battle’ and the like, the superiority of action was already taught.” He answers with “by mixed speech.” A statement that praises action in one place and knowledge in another, seeming to produce doubt, makes my understanding waver between the two, as though you were deluding me. You, who are supremely compassionate, cannot actually be a deluder; nevertheless, because of my confusion it appears to me as though you were. Therefore, determining and stating one beneficial course between the two is what I ask. Alternatively, determine and tell me that one practice by which, when performed, I may attain the good—liberation.

3.translation: The Blessed Lord answers: “In this world.” The meaning is this. If I had taught two mutually independent steadfast paths, knowledge-yoga and karma-yoga, both as means to liberation, then your question—“Tell me one beneficial course between the two”—would be appropriate. But I did not teach them in that way. I taught only one steadfastness in Brahman, expressed in two forms according to differences in qualification, since the two cannot properly exist independently as primary and secondary. Among qualified persons whose inner instruments are respectively pure and impure, the steadfastness directed to liberation is of two kinds. He specifies the two forms. For those of Sāṅkhya—those with pure inner instruments who have ascended the ground of knowledge—steadfastness through knowledge-yoga, meditation and the like, was taught for the ripening of knowledge, as in “having restrained all those senses, sit joined and intent on Me.” For the yogīs who wish to ascend the ground of Sāṅkhya, whose inner instruments are impure and who are qualified for karma-yoga, steadfastness through karma-yoga was taught for the purification of the inner instrument and their ascent to that ground, as in “for a kṣatriya there is nothing higher than a righteous battle.” Therefore both forms of steadfastness were taught solely on the basis of the differing condition—purity or impurity—of the mind: “this understanding has been told to you in Sāṅkhya; hear this one in yoga.”
